passage:
"Sachin, it's six o'clock! Go back to sleep!"
"Can't, didi. Practice."
Kashish pulled the blanket over her head. "It's raining."
"I told the whole class I'd win the hundred metres. In front of Ma'am."
"So?"
"So I have to run." He was already tying his shoes.
"You could just say you were joking."
"I wasn't joking. And everyone heard."
"Yesterday you said your legs were tired."
"Not today."
"Mummy will shout."
"Tell Mummy I'll be back by seven."
Kashish sighed and sat up. "Fine. I'll time you. But if you win, you're buying me chocolate."
"Deal." He grinned and ran out.

qa.q: What race did Sachin tell the class he would win?
qa.a: The hundred metres.

qa.q: Why won't Sachin say he was joking?
qa.a: He feels determined, because he said it aloud in front of the whole class and Ma'am, and he wants his actions to match his word.

qa.q: What choice could Sachin make if he loses the race despite practising?
qa.a: He could tell the class he trained every morning and tried his hardest; being honest about his effort keeps his word better than any excuse.

qa.q: Why might Kashish agree to get up and time him?
qa.a: She may be half annoyed and half impressed by how seriously he takes his promise, and wants to help, especially with chocolate at stake. 😄

grounding: A boy who told his class he would win the race trains in the rain and won't skip practice, because he wants his actions to match his word.

passage: Last month I did something silly. In class, Hafsa said she would win the long jump, so I stood up and said, "I'll win the running race." Everyone clapped. After that, I couldn't stop thinking about it. I'm Nitin, and I'm the boy who usually skips practice. But now everybody knew. So I went every morning. When my friends called me to play cricket after school, I said no and ran laps. I even went to bed early before race day. On race day I came second. I was sad for a bit. But Coach said I had improved more than anyone, and I felt proud, because I really tried to do what I said.

qa.q: What place did Nitin come on race day?
qa.a: Second.

qa.q: Why did Nitin stop skipping practice after the class clapped?
qa.a: He felt determined, and a little pressured, because everyone knew he had said aloud that he would win, and he wanted his actions to match his words.

qa.q: What choice did Nitin make when friends called him to play cricket, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: He said no and ran laps instead, which is how he improved more than anyone, even though he came second.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see Nitin's announcement?
qa.a: Hafsa had just said she would win the long jump, so she might take Nitin's promise as a friendly challenge and notice him training every morning.

passage:
Coach's note — Baljeet, school athletics
Lokesh, class 4, announced at assembly on Monday, "I will win the 200 metres on sports day." Since then he has been first at practice every morning, before even the older boys. On Wednesday it rained and most children stayed home; Lokesh ran in the mud. When I asked why, he said, "I said it in front of everyone. I have to." He is improving fast. I'm pleased, but I'll watch that the promise doesn't turn into fear. I told him that trying his best counts as keeping his word, win or lose. He nodded, then asked for extra starts.

qa.q: When did Lokesh announce he would win the 200 metres?
qa.a: At assembly on Monday.

qa.q: What did Lokesh mean when he said "I have to"?
qa.a: He felt pressured to match his word after announcing his win in front of everyone, so skipping practice felt impossible.

qa.q: What did Coach Baljeet choose to tell Lokesh, and why?
qa.a: That trying his best counts as keeping his word, win or lose, so the promise keeps him working without turning into fear of losing.

qa.q: How might the older boys see Lokesh arriving before them every morning?
qa.a: They might be surprised, amused or even pushed to try harder, seeing a class 4 student so determined.

grounding: A coach notes a boy who publicly promised to win a race and now trains harder than anyone, wanting his actions to match his word.

Tuesday night
Dear Diary,
Today in 5B Ma'am asked who is running the 400 metres on sports day. I stood up and said, 'Me. And I'll win.' Everybody went 'Ooooh.' Even Rishabh, who is fastest.
Now I have to. After school I didn't watch cartoons. I ran round our building six times while Binita Didi timed me on Papa's phone. She laughed and said her little brother runs like a duck. I don't care. On the fifth round my side hurt, but I kept going, because what if someone from 5B saw me stopping?
Tomorrow is Wednesday. I usually skip practice on Wednesday because of drawing class. Not this week. I told Ma'am I'll come.
I said it in front of everyone. So my legs have to say it too.
Divyansh

qa.q: What choice did Divyansh make about Wednesday practice, and why?
qa.a: He decided not to skip it for drawing class, because having said he'd win in front of everyone, he wanted his actions to match his word.

passage: In their village near Hisar, Uday, eleven, had stood up in class and said he would win the 800-metre race at the block sports meet. Now it was wheat-harvest time, and everyone was busy in the fields before sunrise. Still, every morning at five, Uday ran along the canal bank in his school shorts, past the buffaloes and the sleepy chai stall. His sister Pallavi, carrying water to the field, saw him twice one morning. 'Why don't you rest today? Nobody's checking.' 'Everybody heard me,' Uday panted. 'I can't say it and then not do it.' When his friends called him to play gulli-danda one evening, he said no and did his stretches behind the cattle shed. On the day of the meet, Pallavi noticed his old shoes were worn right through at the toes.

qa.a: He ran along the canal bank in his school shorts, past the buffaloes and the sleepy chai stall.

qa.q: What did Uday mean when he said 'I can't say it and then not do it'?
qa.a: He had promised in front of the whole class, so he felt bound to it and would have felt ashamed to skip practice and break his word.

qa.q: Which of Uday's choices showed his public promise was pushing his effort?
qa.a: Running every morning during harvest time and saying no to gulli-danda to do stretches showed he wanted his actions to match what he said.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel when she notices his worn-out shoes?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel proud and touched, seeing how hard her brother worked, and maybe a little worried about his old shoes.

On Monday in the village school, Ojas stood up and told the class, "I'm going to win the running race at the block sports meet." A few boys laughed. Pema, his friend, clapped.
After that, Ojas woke before dawn. He ran on the canal road while mist sat on the fields and the milkman's cycle rattled past. On Thursday it rained. His mother said, "Stay in today." He went anyway, shoes squelching.
Pema met him on the road. "You don't have to kill yourself."
"I said it in front of everyone," Ojas panted. "If I stop now, what was the point of saying it?"
By Saturday he had not missed a single morning. He still wasn't sure he'd win. But he'd kept his word so far.

qa.a: He ran on the canal road.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he said "If I stop now, what was the point of saying it?"
qa.a: He felt determined and pressured, wanting his actions to match what he said in front of the class.

qa.q: What could Pema or his mother say to support Ojas wisely?
qa.a: They could praise his effort and suggest resting on rainy days, reminding him that keeping his word means trying hard, not hurting himself.

qa.q: How might the boys who laughed see Ojas by Saturday?
qa.a: They may start to take him seriously, seeing he hasn't missed a single morning.

passage:
At his school in Seoul, Chen raised his hand on show-and-tell day and said, "I'm going to win the relay race for our class." Everyone looked at him.
After that, Chen changed. At lunch he ate quickly and went to practise baton passes. After school, when Soo-ah invited him to the arcade, he shook his head. "I have to practise."
"It's just one afternoon," Soo-ah said.
"I told the whole class," Chen said. "If I don't practise, I'm a liar."
He ran laps of the playground until the caretaker locked the gate. At home he stretched on the living-room floor while his grandmother watched TV. He didn't know if he'd win. But he wanted what he did to match what he'd said.

qa.q: Where did Soo-ah invite Chen after school?
qa.a: Soo-ah invited him to the arcade.

qa.q: Why does Chen say "If I don't practise, I'm a liar"?
qa.a: He feels pressured and determined, because announcing it to the class made skipping practice feel like breaking his word.

qa.q: What could help Chen keep the promise without burning out?
qa.a: He could keep regular practice but still spend some time with friends, knowing that trying hard is keeping his word.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when Chen keeps saying no?
qa.a: Soo-ah may feel a bit left out and disappointed, missing time with a friend who is suddenly very serious.

grounding: A boy who told his class he would win the relay trains harder and refuses outings so his actions match his word.

Tejas, you told your class you'll win the chess tournament? Good. Now you must practise every day. Why? Let your Ramesh thatha tell you. When I was eleven, I stood up in our village school and said I would win the running race at the temple festival. Everyone heard, even the headmaster.
After that I couldn't sit still. Every morning before the cows were milked, I ran to the river and back. Once I had fever and still wanted to go; my mother stopped me. On race day I didn't win. I came second. But I had never run so hard in my life. Because I'd said it out loud, my legs had to keep my word.
So tell me, how many games will you play this week?

passage: The Diwali holidays had begun, and the Pune colony smelled of oil lamps and firecracker smoke. On Friday Siddharth had told his whole class that he would win the 50-metre freestyle at the inter-school meet. Now his cousin Pankaj stood at the door with a box of sparklers. 'Come! Everyone's in the parking. Skip swimming for one day.' Siddharth stared at the sparklers for a long time. 'I told the class I'm going to win,' he said. 'If I skip, I'm just a talker.' He grabbed his goggles and cycled to the club pool, where only two old uncles were doing slow laps. He swam twenty lengths, slapping the wall hard each time. That night he came home with wrinkled fingers, and Pankaj had saved him the last sparkler.

'Yash, it's pouring! You're not cycling today.'
'I have to, Gargi Didi. The race is in two weeks.'
'It's a school race. You don't have to win.'
'I told the whole class I'd win. In front of Ma'am.'
'So?'
'So if I sit home eating pakodas, I lied.'
'You'll slip in the mud.'
'I'll go round the building parking. It has a roof.'
'Twenty rounds of a parking?'
'Thirty.'
Gargi sighed. 'Fine. I'm timing you. And if your chest hurts, you stop.'
'Deal.' Yash already had his helmet on.
Twenty minutes later Gargi shouted down the stairs, 'Thirty! Now come and eat.'
Yash wheeled in, soaked with sweat, grinning. 'Tomorrow, thirty-five.'

qa.q: Where did Yash cycle because of the rain?
qa.a: Round the building parking, which has a roof.

qa.q: Why did Yash insist on cycling in the monsoon rain?
qa.a: Yash felt determined and a little anxious about looking like a liar; having told the whole class he would win, skipping practice felt wrong.

qa.a: Gargi agreed to time him and set a safety rule; she could also remind him that trying hard counts even if he doesn't win.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel watching Yash push for thirty-five rounds?
qa.a: Gargi may feel both proud of his effort and a little worried that he is putting too much weight on one promise.

passage: In January, before the Republic Day sports meet, I did something big. In front of the whole class, I said, "I'm going to win the 200 metres." Everyone went "Ooooh."
